subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Tracing the Godavari: Map Reading and River Geography
periods.section_ref: Where I Begin, Where I Flow
periods.textbook_anchor: Where I Begin, Where I Flow — Identify states Godavari flows through, a dam and wildlife sanctuary along it, and tributaries that join it (p. 22)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map image of the Godavari river system (p. 22)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening poem in the chapter, then invites students to close their eyes and imagine they are a river beginning as a tiny stream high in the mountains. A brief oral exchange follows: where might such a stream start, and where might it end? Students share ideas freely.

Students open Textbook p. 22 and study the map of the Godavari river system carefully. Working individually in their notebooks, they respond to the three questions printed alongside the map — naming the states the river flows through, identifying a dam and a wildlife sanctuary along its course, and listing tributaries that join it.

Pairs compare their answers and discuss any differences. The teacher brings the class together on a quick board summary: source at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats, the river's 1,465-kilometre journey, the name Dakshina Ganga, the Godavari Pushkaram festival at Nashik, and the final meeting with the Bay of Bengal. Students add any details they missed to their notebooks.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks completing this prompt: 'The Godavari matters to people because…' — drawing only on what they read and discussed. Two or three students share aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can read a river map to identify geographical features such as source, tributaries, dams, and the river's meeting with the sea.
periods.section_context: Godavari river source at Trimbakeshwar, Western Ghats, states the river flows through, tributaries, a dam, a wildlife sanctuary, Bay of Bengal, Dakshina Ganga, Godavari Pushkaram festival, Nashik.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think this river is called Dakshina Ganga — what does that name tell us about how people feel about it?' Draw out the sacred and cultural significance naturally alongside the geographical features.

periods.activity_title: River Habitats: Observing the Life Godavari Holds
periods.textbook_anchor: The Life I Hold — Observe and distinguish the forest and delta habitats of the Godavari and the wildlife each supports (p. 22)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of Godavari forest and Coringa Mangrove delta habitats

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses an opening question: 'What kinds of living things do you think a large river and its surrounding land could support?' Students call out ideas; the teacher lists them on the board without correcting yet. This surfaces prior knowledge and curiosity.

Students read the section 'The Life I Hold' in their textbooks, studying any accompanying illustrations. They draw a two-column table in their notebooks headed 'Forest Along the River' and 'Delta and Mangrove' and record the plants and animals named in each habitat — tiger, barking deer, Indian golden gecko, red sandalwood in the forests; Coringa Mangrove Forests at the delta where freshwater meets the sea.

Class discussion: the teacher introduces the distinction between a perennial river (flowing year-round) and a seasonal river (flowing only in the rainy season), asking students to give reasons why the Godavari is perennial and why that matters for the wildlife that depends on it. Students note the key distinction in their tables.

Students sketch one creature from the Godavari forest and one from the delta in their notebooks and label its habitat. A quick sharing round invites students to say one thing that surprised them about the life this river holds.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify living things by the specific habitat zones within a river system and explain why perennial flow supports greater biodiversity.
periods.section_context: Perennial river, seasonal river, Godavari forest habitat, tiger, barking deer, Indian golden gecko, red sandalwood, Coringa Mangrove Forests, delta, freshwater meeting the sea.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'If the river stopped flowing for several months every year, which of these animals do you think would be most affected, and why?' This encourages reasoning about habitat dependency rather than simple recall.

periods.activity_title: Rivers and Livelihoods: Discussion and Connection
periods.section_ref: The Many Ways I Support Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: The Many Ways I Support Lives — Reflect on why people have always built homes near rivers or water bodies (p. 24)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of rice cultivation and river-side settlements (p. 24–26)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 24 and read the question about why people have always built homes near rivers. Before writing, they turn to a partner and share their first instinct. The teacher invites three or four pairs to share aloud, charting the emerging reasons on the board.

The class reads the section 'The Many Ways I Support Lives' together. The teacher pauses at the textbook illustrations of rice fields, fishermen, and riverside towns (Textbook pp. 24–26), asking students to name what they see and connect it to the river. Students then write individual responses in notebooks to the questions on p. 25: three ways people depend on Godavari, and the occupations people near the river are engaged in.

A structured whole-class discussion connects the local to the wider picture: the teacher asks which of these dependencies — drinking water, irrigation, fishing, ecotourism — students have seen in their own area or heard about from family. Students share personal connections. The teacher notes that rivers have supported human settlements since ancient times, linking to the idea that water access shaped where towns and cities grew.

Students write one sentence each in notebooks answering Textbook p. 26: which crops grow near the Godavari, and what water source their own region's crops use. Two or three students share, inviting comparison across the class.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain multiple ways a river supports human livelihoods and connect those uses to settlement patterns and occupations in their own region.
periods.section_context: River as water source for drinking, cooking, washing, irrigation, industrial use; rice cultivation; fishing; ecotourism; Godavari riverside towns and villages; ancient settlement near rivers; crops near Godavari.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone's family ever lived near a river or a well — why did they choose that place?' Drawing out lived family experience makes the near-to-far connection concrete. Invite students to mention any traditional water-drawing or irrigation practices they may have seen.

periods.section_ref: The Many Ways I Support Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: The Many Ways I Support Lives — Make a poster showing all the ways rivers help people, including homes, farms, boats, and fishermen (p. 26)
materials: Large paper or chart paper (one per group)

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly recaps the river-dependency ideas from the discussion on livelihoods, asking students to name uses rapidly. Groups of four are formed. The teacher explains that each group will make a poster as described in Textbook p. 26 — showing all the ways rivers help people — and that every drawing must be labelled.

Groups plan and draw their posters. Each poster must show at least four distinct uses (e.g., drinking water, irrigation, fishing, transport) with small illustrations and labels. The teacher circulates, asking each group to add at least one detail they discovered from the textbook text rather than only from memory — encouraging them to flip back through Textbook pp. 24–26.
Groups do a brief gallery walk — each group's poster is placed where others can view it. Students note on a slip of paper one item another group included that their own group did not.
Quick whole-class share: each group names the one new detail they noticed. The teacher affirms the breadth of river support for human life and collects or displays the posters in the classroom.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent, through labelled drawings, the range of ways a river supports human life and livelihoods.
periods.section_context: Poster showing river uses: drinking water, cooking, washing, irrigation, fishing, ecotourism, transport; homes, farms, boats, fishermen near Godavari.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt groups: 'Can you add something to your poster that shows how people have always — even long ago — relied on rivers?' This invites students to draw traditional practices such as drawing water from a river or using a canal without the teacher labelling it.

periods.section_ref: Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow
periods.textbook_anchor: Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow — Identify what problems arise after a dam is built and how they might be solved (p. 27)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram or image of a dam and reservoir (p. 27)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a scenario: 'Imagine a river that floods every rainy season and then dries up in summer. What could be built to help store that water?' Students share ideas. The teacher guides toward the concept of a dam and writes the word on the board. Students open Textbook p. 27 and read the section independently.

Students draw a simple T-chart in their notebooks: 'What a dam provides' versus 'What a dam takes away or changes.' Working individually first, then comparing with a neighbour, they populate both columns from the textbook text — stored water for drinking, irrigation, and electricity on one side; flooded land, displaced wildlife and people on the other.

A structured whole-class discussion on the trade-off: the teacher reads the textbook question 'What problems can arise after a dam is built? How can they be solved?' (p. 27) aloud, and students discuss in groups of three before sharing with the class. The teacher records diverse solutions on the board — resettlement plans, wildlife corridors, compensation — without endorsing a single answer, modelling that complex problems have multiple partial solutions.

Students write their personal response to the textbook question in their notebooks. The teacher invites two or three students to read their responses, emphasising that reasonable people can weigh the same trade-offs differently.

periods.implied_lo: Students can weigh the benefits and costs of a large humanmade water-management structure and propose ways to address the problems it creates.
periods.section_context: Dams in India (more than 900), reservoir, stored water for dry seasons, drinking water, irrigation, electricity generation; flooded land, displacement of wildlife and people.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you know of a dam near your state or region? Have you heard any stories about families who had to move because of it?' Drawing on local knowledge deepens the trade-off discussion beyond the textbook example.

periods.activity_title: Solubility Experiment — Visible and Invisible Pollutants
periods.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
periods.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — Observe what happens when sugar is added to one glass of water and cooking oil to another, and compare which appears clear (p. 29)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of a healthy river versus an algae-covered river (p. 30)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the question: 'If something harmful was mixed into a river, would you always be able to see it?' Students share predictions. The teacher introduces the word 'solubility' simply — some things dissolve in water and disappear from sight, others do not — and explains today's inquiry.

Groups of three set up the experiment from Textbook p. 29: two clear glasses of water, a spoonful of sugar stirred into one and a spoonful of cooking oil stirred into the other. Students observe and record in their notebooks: which glass looks clear, which looks changed, and what this might mean for water safety. The teacher asks guiding questions as they work — 'Which one would you know was contaminated just by looking?'

Class discussion of observations. The teacher connects the results to real pollutants: fertiliser runoff dissolves like sugar (invisible, yet causes algal overgrowth — the 'green blanket' effect), while oil spills are visible but also harmful. Students look at Textbook p. 30 and answer the printed questions about the two river images — healthy river versus algae-covered river — in their notebooks.

Students write three things they personally throw in the waste bin that, if they reached a river, would harm aquatic life or people — connecting the list-making task from Textbook p. 29 to their own daily choices. One or two students share.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple solubility inquiry, distinguish visible from dissolved pollutants, and explain how each type harms a water body.
periods.section_context: Sugar dissolved in water (invisible, clear), cooking oil in water (visible), solubility, fertiliser runoff, algal overgrowth ('green blanket' effect), plastic wrappers and bags in rivers, Namami Gange programme.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What soaps or floor cleaners are used in your home — where does that water go after washing?' This draws out T-10 naturally and helps students connect household choices to river health without a lecture.

periods.activity_title: Flood Safety — Matching Consequences and Civic Role-Play
periods.textbook_anchor: When a River Floods — Match flood problems to what each affects: shelter, safe drinking water, learning, travel, electricity, health, and food supply (p. 32)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Has anyone seen images or news of a flood — what did you notice had happened to the homes, roads, and fields?' Students share observations. The teacher introduces the key idea that deforestation worsens flooding because tree cover slows rainwater runoff, and asks students to think about why that is.

Students open Textbook p. 32 and complete the match-the-columns activity individually in their notebooks — linking each flood problem (dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut) to what it affects (safe drinking, travel and transport, food supply, lights fans and phones, people's health, shelter, learning). Pairs compare and resolve any differences.

Students read the Flood Safety Tips infographic on Textbook pp. 33–34 in groups of four. Each group then conducts a short role-play: one student is the Sarpanch or Municipal Corporator deciding actions before, during, and after a flood — including keeping elderly people, people with disability, and animals safe. Other group members ask questions as community members. Groups need no props; the discussion itself is the activity.

Brief class reflection: each group shares one decision their Sarpanch made that surprised them or felt most important. The teacher connects these decisions to what organised disaster preparedness looks like in real civic life.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect specific flood events to their cascading effects on daily life and propose safety or preparedness actions for a community.
periods.section_context: River flooding causes, deforestation worsening floods, flood effects — dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut; Flood Safety Tips before/during/after; civic preparedness for elderly, people with disability, and animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt the role-play by asking: 'What would you tell a family with a very old grandparent to do before the flood water reaches the street?' This grounds abstract preparedness in specific human situations.

periods.activity_title: When Water Runs Out — Imagining and Reflecting on Scarcity
periods.textbook_anchor: When a River Runs Dry! — Reflect on what you would do if there were no water in your home for an entire day, and then for a week (p. 35)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the textbook scenario aloud: no water in the home for an entire day. Students close their eyes and think for a moment about their morning routine — waking up, brushing teeth, cooking breakfast. The teacher then opens the floor: 'What would be the very first thing you would miss?' Students share, one after another, without evaluation.

Students respond individually in notebooks to the two questions on Textbook p. 35 — what would they do with no water for a day, and for a week (bathing, drinking, cooking, cleaning, finding water). The teacher then shares briefly the Chennai 2019 water crisis and Bengaluru 2022 contrast from the textbook, so students see that these are not imaginary situations.

A structured reflection discussion: the teacher asks students to think of water-wasting habits in their own daily life — running taps, leaving water in plates, long showers — and to say aloud one change they personally could make. The teacher introduces the National Water Mission and water ATMs as examples of organised conservation effort, asking students whether they have seen or heard of anything similar near them.

Students write a personal conservation commitment in their notebooks: one water-wasting habit they have noticed in themselves and one concrete action they will try. Two or three students share. The teacher affirms that individual habits and civic systems both matter for water security.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the human consequences of water scarcity, reflect on their own water-use habits, and identify personal conservation actions.
periods.section_context: No water for a day and for a week scenarios, bathing, drinking, cooking, cleaning, finding water; Chennai 2019 water crisis; Bengaluru 2022 floods; National Water Mission; water ATMs; personal water-wasting habits; individual and civic conservation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you know of anyone — perhaps in your family or neighbourhood — who has had to fetch water from far away? What was that experience like?' This surfaces lived experiences of water scarcity and makes the reflection visceral rather than abstract.

periods.activity_title: Water Filter Design — Simple Inquiry and Prototyping
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Design a simple water filter using everyday materials and explain the purpose of each material included (p. 37)
materials: Dirty or muddy water (prepared by the teacher)

time_bands.activity: The teacher shows students a cup of muddy water and asks: 'If you had to make this water cleaner using only things you can find at home or school, what would you use?' Students brainstorm aloud. The teacher introduces Textbook p. 37 Task on designing a simple water filter and explains that groups will build and test a rough prototype today.

Groups of three plan their filter design on paper first — listing each layer or material and giving a reason for including it (e.g., gravel to catch large particles, sand for smaller ones, cloth or cotton wool for finer matter). They then build a quick prototype using the available materials — layering chosen materials in a cup or bottle with a small hole — and pour a small amount of muddy water through it, observing the output.

Groups compare their designs and results: which filter produced clearer output? What would they change in a second attempt? The teacher facilitates a discussion connecting their observations to the broader idea that clean water does not appear automatically — it requires deliberate effort, whether by a simple filter, a water treatment plant, or the Namami Gange programme.

Each student writes two sentences in their notebook: what their filter did well and one change they would make if they had more materials. The teacher collects the written plans as a record of their inquiry thinking.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and test a simple filtration system, explain the function of each component, and evaluate its effectiveness against an observed outcome.
periods.section_context: Simple water filter design, everyday materials (sand, gravel, cloth or cotton wool), muddy water, layered filtration, evaluating filter output, connecting to organised water treatment efforts.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do any of you know of traditional ways people used to clean or store water — perhaps a clay pot, a sand filter, or a well with a specific lining?' This invites students to share family or community knowledge without the teacher labelling it.

periods.activity_title: A River of Our Own — Local Rivers, Family Stories, and a Rule to Protect Them
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Imagine planning a new city near a river: what steps would you take to keep the river clean, prevent floods, and ensure water for everyone? (p. 37)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to name a river that flows through their state or near their home. Students share names; the teacher lists them on the board. Each student who names a river adds one use or one story they have heard about it. This surfaces the diversity of river relationships across the class.

Students open Textbook p. 37 and choose one of two tasks to respond to in their notebooks: (a) write about a story or festival related to rivers in their region that a family member has shared with them, or (b) write what an elder told them about how rivers near their home have changed over the years. Students who do not have a family story to share may write about what they imagine a grandparent might say about a river they have read about in this chapter.

Students work on the city-planning task from Textbook p. 37 — imagining they are planning a new city near a river and deciding three things: how to keep the river clean, how to prevent floods during heavy rain, and how to ensure enough water for everyone even in summer. They write their plan in their notebooks, drawing a simple sketch of the city layout if they wish.

Each student writes one rule they would create to protect rivers in their city or village — as asked in Textbook p. 37 — and reads it aloud. The teacher closes by affirming that rivers are living systems that need both natural conditions and active human care to thrive, and that every student in the room has the knowledge to be a steward of the rivers near them.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect the natural and human dimensions of a river to their own region, articulate a personal conservation rule, and plan civic water-management measures.
periods.section_context: Local rivers in students' states, family stories and festivals related to rivers, elder accounts of river change, imagined city planning near a river (keeping river clean, preventing floods, ensuring water in summer), one personal rule to protect rivers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you were the Sarpanch or Mayor of a new city, which of the problems we have studied — pollution, flooding, or drought — would you tackle first, and why?' Encourage students to justify their priority using evidence from the chapter.

assessment_items.question_text:
Look at the statements below about the Godavari river. Which one correctly describes a geographical feature of its journey?
A. Godavari begins at the source of the Ganga in the Himalayas and flows westward to the Arabian Sea.
B. Godavari begins as a stream at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats and flows east to meet the Bay of Bengal.
C. Godavari is a seasonal river that flows only during the monsoon season and dries up each winter.
D. Godavari flows entirely within one state and has no tributaries joining its course.

options.label: A
options.text: Godavari begins at the source of the Ganga in the Himalayas and flows westward to the Arabian Sea.

options.label: B
options.text: Godavari begins as a stream at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats and flows east to meet the Bay of Bengal.

options.label: C
options.text: Godavari is a seasonal river that flows only during the monsoon season and dries up each winter.

options.label: D
options.text: Godavari flows entirely within one state and has no tributaries joining its course.

assessment_items.annotation: Award 1 mark for B. No partial credit.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Where I Begin, Where I Flow
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a river map to identify geographical features such as source, tributaries, dams, and the river's meeting with the sea.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the Godavari with the Ganga — the student has mixed up the two rivers or their sources and direction of flow.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses perennial with seasonal river — the student has not grasped the distinction introduced in 'The Life I Hold' section.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Does not recognise that the Godavari flows through multiple states and gathers tributaries — a failure to read the map task on p. 22.

assessment_items.question_text: The Godavari river passes through forests and ends in a delta before reaching the sea. Name two animals found in the forests along the Godavari and explain why a perennial river is better for wildlife than a seasonal river.
expected_elements: Names two animals from the Godavari forest habitat (any two from: tiger, barking deer, Indian golden gecko).
States that a perennial river flows throughout the year, unlike a seasonal river which flows only during the rainy season.
Explains that year-round water availability supports wildlife by providing a reliable drinking source, habitat, and food chain continuity.
assessment_items.annotation: Award up to 3 marks: 1 for each correct animal name (max 1 mark combined for both), 1 for the perennial/seasonal distinction, 1 for the wildlife benefit explanation. Accept any well-reasoned benefit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify living things by the specific habitat zones within a river system and explain why perennial flow supports greater biodiversity.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Names two animals from the Godavari forest habitat (any two from: tiger, barking deer, Indian golden gecko).
States that a perennial river flows throughout the year, unlike a seasonal river which flows only during the rainy season.
Explains that year-round water availability supports wildlife by providing a reliable drinking source, habitat, and food chain continuity.

assessment_items.question_text:
People have built their homes near rivers since ancient times. Which of the following best explains why settlements grew near rivers?
A. Rivers provide land that is always flat, which makes it easier to build large buildings.
B. Rivers provide water for drinking, irrigation, and other daily needs, supporting farming and fishing.
C. Rivers keep the air cool all year round, making the climate comfortable for people to live in.
D. Rivers produce electricity, so people living near them never face power cuts.

options.label: A
options.text: Rivers provide land that is always flat, which makes it easier to build large buildings.

options.label: B
options.text: Rivers provide water for drinking, irrigation, and other daily needs, supporting farming and fishing.

options.label: C
options.text: Rivers keep the air cool all year round, making the climate comfortable for people to live in.

options.label: D
options.text: Rivers produce electricity, so people living near them never face power cuts.

assessment_items.annotation: Award 1 mark for B. No partial credit.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Many Ways I Support Lives
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain multiple ways a river supports human livelihoods and connect those uses to settlement patterns and occupations in their own region.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Focuses on land topology rather than water access — the student has not connected rivers to the water-dependent livelihoods discussed in the section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Offers a plausible but incorrect reason — the student may be guessing based on a general feeling about rivers rather than the textbook content.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Overgeneralises the electricity benefit of dams — the student has conflated one specific function (hydroelectricity) with the primary reason for ancient settlements, which predate dams.

assessment_items.task: Draw a poster that shows at least four different ways a river helps people. Label each drawing clearly.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Think about: Who uses the river for food? Who uses it for water? What work do people do near the river? What do farms near the river grow?
Draw a picture for each idea and write a label (one or two words) next to it.
format_of_output: A drawn poster with at least four labelled illustrations of river uses
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the poster on breadth (at least four distinct uses shown), clarity of labelling, and whether the drawings accurately represent a river use from the chapter. Accept any correctly labelled river use; do not penalise artistic quality.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Many Ways I Support Lives
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent, through labelled drawings, the range of ways a river supports human life and livelihoods.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can retrieve and visually communicate multiple functions of a river for human life, moving from text-based knowledge to a creative representational format.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts students to think across the four categories of river use (food, water, work, farming) before drawing. A student who draws fewer than four items may have followed only part of the scaffold.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: four or more clearly labelled, distinct uses (e.g., drinking water, irrigation, fishing, transport), accurate representations. Weak: fewer than four uses, unlabelled drawings, or uses that do not relate to rivers (e.g., roads).
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may write labels in boxes instead. Students who cannot label in English may label in their home language — the teacher can verify understanding orally.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The task mirrors the textbook's own poster activity and consolidates visual-representational learning, which is core to the C&E dominant mode of the unit.

assessment_items.question_text: A dam is being planned on a large river. Some people say it will bring great benefits; others say it will cause serious harm. Explain two benefits and two problems that could arise from building the dam. Then suggest one way to reduce one of the problems.
look_for: Names two distinct benefits (any two from: water storage for dry seasons, supply of drinking water, irrigation for farms, generation of electricity).
Names two distinct problems (any two from: flooding of land and villages, displacement of people, loss of wildlife habitat, disruption of river ecosystem).
Proposes a realistic solution to one named problem (e.g., building resettlement homes for displaced families, creating wildlife corridors, compensating farmers for lost land).
Shows understanding that dam construction involves a genuine trade-off, not a purely good or purely bad outcome.
Uses chapter vocabulary (dam, reservoir, displacement, irrigation, electricity) accurately in context.
assessment_items.annotation: Award up to 5 marks: 1 per clearly stated benefit (max 2), 1 per clearly stated problem (max 2), 1 for a plausible and specific solution. A student who states only benefits or only problems without the trade-off perspective can score a maximum of 3.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can weigh the benefits and costs of a large humanmade water-management structure and propose ways to address the problems it creates.

assessment_items.question_text: A student dissolves a spoonful of sugar in a glass of water and adds a spoonful of cooking oil to another glass of water. She stirs both. The sugar-water looks clear; the oil-water looks cloudy. What does this experiment tell us about pollution in rivers? Give one example of a pollutant that dissolves in river water and one that does not, and explain why both types are harmful.
expected_elements: States that some pollutants dissolve in water and become invisible, while others do not dissolve and remain visible.
Gives a correctly categorised example of a dissolving pollutant (e.g., fertiliser runoff, chemical waste, soap or detergent).
Gives a correctly categorised example of a non-dissolving pollutant (e.g., oil, plastic).

Explains that dissolved pollutants are harmful because they cannot be seen yet make water unsafe to drink or cause algal overgrowth; non-dissolved pollutants harm animals that may ingest them or block water flow.
assessment_items.annotation: Award up to 4 marks: 1 for the dissolving/non-dissolving distinction, 1 for each correct pollutant example with category (max 2), 1 for a valid harm explanation covering both types. Accept any scientifically correct pollutant not explicitly in the chapter if the student provides a correct reason.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple solubility inquiry, distinguish visible from dissolved pollutants, and explain how each type harms a water body.

assessment_items.question_text: Heavy rains caused a river near a village to flood. The Sarpanch received the following list of problems: dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut. Choose any three problems from this list and explain what aspect of daily life each one disrupts most seriously for the people of the village.
expected_elements: Selects three problems from the given list (dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut).

For each problem, names the specific aspect of life disrupted — e.g., dirty water affects safe drinking, broken roads affect travel and transport, lost crops affect food supply, no electricity affects lights/fans/phones, spread of diseases affects people's health, damaged homes affect shelter, schools shut affect learning.
Explains each disruption in at least one complete sentence showing understanding of why it matters to daily life.
assessment_items.annotation: Award up to 3 marks, one per correctly explained problem-disruption pair. The student need not use the exact labels from the textbook matching task — accept any accurate explanation of why the problem matters.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect specific flood events to their cascading effects on daily life and propose safety or preparedness actions for a community.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

expected_elements: Selects three problems from the given list (dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut).

Explains each disruption in at least one complete sentence showing understanding of why it matters to daily life.

assessment_items.task: Think about your own water use today — from morning to night. Identify two ways in which you waste water without meaning to. For each one, write one thing you will do differently to save water.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Think about: brushing teeth, washing hands, cooking, bathing, drinking, watering plants.
For each water-wasting habit you identify, complete this sentence: 'Instead of _______, I will _______.'
format_of_output: Two written sentences in the 'Instead of / I will' format
Or a short paragraph describing two habits and two changes
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two genuine water-wasting habits and any realistic conservation substitutions. Do not penalise if the habits are small — the assessment values honest self-reflection and a plausible action. Regional variation in water-use practices is expected and acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the human consequences of water scarcity, reflect on their own water-use habits, and identify personal conservation actions.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can connect the concept of water scarcity to personal daily behaviour and translate that awareness into a concrete, self-chosen conservation action.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold steers students to specific daily water-use moments (brushing, bathing, cooking) so they do not give vague answers. A student who writes 'I waste water sometimes' without specifics has not engaged with the scaffold.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: two specific, named habits (e.g., 'I leave the tap running while brushing') paired with concrete alternatives ('I will turn it off between rinses'). Weak: vague habits, implausible solutions, or a single habit repeated twice.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may respond in the form of a drawing with labels if writing is difficult. Students whose homes have very limited water access may describe what they observe others doing — the spirit of the task is self-awareness, not judgment.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Short written reflection (sentence pairs or paragraph)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The sentence-pair scaffold makes the reflection structured and executable within a single sitting while still requiring genuine personal reasoning.

assessment_items.question_text: A student built a simple water filter using layers of gravel, sand, and cotton cloth and poured muddy water through it. The water that came out was less muddy but still slightly cloudy. (a) Explain what each layer in the filter does. (b) Suggest one change to the filter that might make the output cleaner, and give a reason for your suggestion.
expected_elements: Explains that gravel catches large particles, sand traps smaller particles, and cotton cloth or fabric filters the finest particles — each layer has a distinct role in reducing muddiness.
Identifies a specific improvement (e.g., adding a thicker sand layer, using finer cloth, adding a charcoal layer, repeating the filtration) rather than a vague one.
Gives a reason for the suggested improvement that connects to how the filter works (e.g., 'A thicker sand layer would trap more small particles that passed through the first time').
assessment_items.annotation: Award up to 3 marks: 1 for correctly explaining the role of each layer (all three must be mentioned for full credit; 0.5 for two layers explained), 1 for a specific and named improvement, 1 for a reasoned justification. Do not penalise students who suggest charcoal — it is scientifically valid even if not in the textbook.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and test a simple filtration system, explain the function of each component, and evaluate its effectiveness against an observed outcome.

assessment_items.question_text: You are planning a new city near a river. The river sometimes floods in heavy rain and sometimes runs very low in summer. Explain three things you would plan for your city to: (a) keep the river clean, (b) prevent flood damage, and (c) ensure enough water for everyone even in dry months. Use what you know about rivers, pollution, floods, and water conservation to support your ideas.
look_for: Proposes a specific and plausible measure to keep the river clean (e.g., treating sewage before it enters the river, preventing factory waste discharge, placing waste bins away from the riverbank, community clean-up rules).

Proposes a specific flood-prevention or flood-damage-reduction measure (e.g., planting trees along river banks to slow runoff, building flood barriers or embankments, creating early warning systems, designating safe evacuation routes).

Proposes a specific water-conservation or storage measure for dry months (e.g., building a small reservoir or check dam, rainwater harvesting, limiting water use, installing water ATMs for equitable distribution).
Shows understanding that rivers are shared resources requiring both natural management and civic planning.
Demonstrates awareness of trade-offs — e.g., acknowledging that a dam stores water but can displace communities, or that factories provide jobs but must manage their waste.
assessment_items.annotation: Award up to 5 marks: 1 per clearly stated and plausible measure (max 3, one per sub-part), 1 for demonstrating understanding of rivers as shared civic resources, 1 for acknowledging any trade-off. Accept regionally varied answers — a student proposing traditional rainwater harvesting tanks or community wells is equally valid. Regional variation in conservation practices is expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect the natural and human dimensions of a river to their own region, articulate a personal conservation rule, and plan civic water-management measures.
